title: Inventory planning software: what it covers, how to choose
summary: Inventory planning software sets stock targets, reorder points, and allocation. McKinsey found early AI adopters cut inventory 35%. How to evaluate it.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 14 October 2026.


Inventory planning software works out how much stock each product should hold at each location, when to reorder it, and how much to order, using a demand forecast, supplier lead times, and a service level target. It is worth buying when your stock decisions outgrow the spreadsheet that holds the rules together, and only if it plans at the level where those decisions are actually made.


Noor plans stock for a home décor retailer with 60 stores. Her reorder rules lived in a workbook with one safety stock percentage per category. When a ceramic lamp line sold 40% faster than forecast in October, the workbook kept recommending the same order quantity for every lamp, in every store, for three weeks. (Noor is an illustrative example.) The formulas were fine, but the workbook could not see that one rule suited a fast variant in a city store and a slow one in a small-town store.


This guide covers what inventory planning software does, how it differs from inventory management systems, what to check before you buy, and where it falls short. If you would rather see inventory planning software on real data, you can[run a planning test on your own product data](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


> **Key Takeaways**
>
>
> - Inventory planning software turns a forecast, lead times, and a service level into stock targets and order recommendations. For a product selling 12 units a day with a 10 day lead time, the worked example below gives a reorder point of 141 units.
> - IHL Group estimated in September 2025 that inventory distortion, the combined cost of out-of-stocks and overstocks, reaches $1.73 trillion a year, or 6.5% of global retail sales.
> - McKinsey reports that early adopters of AI-enabled supply chain management cut inventory levels by 35% compared with slower-moving competitors. The method and time period are not disclosed, so treat 35% as a ceiling, not a target.
> - Six checks separate a planning tool you can rely on from one that repeats your spreadsheet: planning granularity, lead time handling, forecast transparency, data connection, exception workflow, and time to first plan.
> - A pilot on one category over 6 to 8 weeks, compared with what buyers actually ordered, tells you more than any demo.


## What is inventory planning software?


Inventory planning software is a tool that decides how much stock to hold for each product at each location, when to reorder, and how much to order. It combines a demand forecast with lead times, service level targets, and cost limits to produce stock targets and purchase or transfer recommendations, which planners review and approve.


The word planning matters. The tool looks forward, from a forecast, and recommends decisions before stock runs short or piles up. A system that only records what you hold and what you sold sits in a different category, and most retailers already have one.


The scale of the problem explains why retailers invest here. IHL Group’s September 2025 analysis puts inventory distortion at $1.73 trillion a year, or 6.5% of global retail sales. The report gives the combined figure rather than a split between overstock and out-of-stock, so it shows the size of the gap without telling you which side your own business sits on.


## What does inventory planning software cover?


Inventory planning software covers five jobs, and the quality of the whole depends on how well the first one feeds the others.


1. **Demand input.** A forecast by product and location, built from sales history, seasonality, promotions, and events. This is the signal everything else uses. For a closer look at what a good forecast needs, see how Metreecs approaches[AI demand planning](https://www.metreecs.com/demand-planning) .
2. **Stock targets.** Safety stock, reorder points, and minimum and maximum levels, derived from demand variability, lead time, and the service level you want.
3. **Replenishment.** Order timing and quantities, including supplier constraints such as case packs and minimum order values.
4. **Allocation.** Where stock should go across warehouses and stores, including transfers when one location sells through and another does not.
5. **Monitoring.** Exceptions that flag products drifting away from plan, so planners look at 30 problems rather than 3,000 products.


### A worked example


Take one product that sells 12 units a day on average, with a daily standard deviation of 4 units, a supplier lead time of 10 days, and a 95% service level target (a z-score of 1.65). Demand over the lead time is 12 times 10, or 120 units. Safety stock is 1.65 times 4 times the square root of 10, which is about 21 units. The reorder point is 120 plus 21, or 141 units.


A spreadsheet can do this for one product. The difficulty is doing it for 8,000 product and variant combinations across 60 locations, then refreshing it weekly as demand and lead times move. That repetition is the job the software takes over. For a wider view of the ordering side, our article on[how AI is reinventing replenishment](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/how-ai-is-reinventing-replenishment) walks through it.


Across Metreecs’ work with retailers, one mistake we repeatedly see is applying a single safety stock rule to a whole category, which overstocks slow variants and starves fast ones in the same breath.


## How is inventory planning software different from inventory management software?


Inventory management software records stock: what you hold, where, and what moved. Inventory planning software decides what you should hold and what to do next. Most retailers need both, and the planning tool reads from the management system rather than replacing it.


Dimension Inventory management software Inventory planning software


Core question What do I have, and where is it? What should I hold, and what should I order?


Time view Present and past Future, from a forecast


Typical data Stock counts, receipts, transfers, sales Forecast, lead times, service targets, costs


Output Accurate records, pick and receive tasks Stock targets, orders, transfers, exceptions


Usual owner Operations, warehouse, store teams Planning, buying, supply chain


The boundary blurs at the edges, since many enterprise resource planning (ERP) and warehouse systems include a basic reorder point feature. That feature usually takes one fixed number per product. Planning tools recalculate it as demand and lead times change. When the targets themselves become the lever for freeing cash, the topic overlaps with[inventory optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/inventory-optimization) , which adds the trade-off between service level and capital tied up in stock.


## How to evaluate inventory planning software


Evaluate inventory planning software on how it behaves with your data, not on its feature list. Every vendor lists forecasting, safety stock, and replenishment. The differences show up in six places, and each one can be tested in a demo.


Check What to ask Red flag


Planning granularity Does it plan by product, variant, and location, or by category and region? Category-level targets that are split down afterwards


Lead time handling Does it use actual supplier lead times and their variability? One fixed lead time per supplier


Forecast transparency Can a planner see why a recommendation changed? A single number with no drivers or error history


Data connection How does it read from your ERP, point of sale, and e-commerce data, and how often? Manual file uploads as the main route


Exception workflow Does it surface the products that need attention, with reasons? Long lists of every product, unranked


Time to first plan How long until recommendations run on your own data? A multi-month setup before any plan appears


Callum is a buying manager at a beauty brand with 35 stores and a growing online channel. He shortlisted three tools and asked each to plan the same 200 products from his last season’s data. Two returned category-level targets, while the third produced a reorder point per product and store and flagged 14 products where its recommendation differed from his team’s order by more than 25%. (Callum is an illustrative example.) He spent his review time on those 14, not on all 200, and that mattered more to him than any feature on the sheet.


The planners we work with often underestimate how much of a rollout is data connection rather than modelling. Product master data, supplier lead times, and stock position usually need cleaning before any model can read them reliably, so ask each vendor what they need from you in the first month.


## Where does inventory planning software fall short?


Inventory planning software improves decisions that are already possible to make. It has limits, and knowing them early makes a pilot easier to judge.


**It depends on the inputs.** Wrong lead times, duplicate product records, or stock counts that drift from reality produce confident but wrong recommendations. The software cannot tell that a supplier promises 10 days and delivers in 17.


**It struggles where history is thin.** New products and very slow sellers give the model little to learn from. New product forecasting needs a separate approach based on similar products and attributes.


**It cannot fix a buying process that ignores it.** If recommendations are overridden by habit every week, the plan and the purchase orders diverge, and the software gets blamed for a workflow problem. Tracking how often planners accept or change recommendations is a useful early signal.


**Published benefit figures are ceilings.** McKinsey’s 35% inventory reduction for early AI adopters compares leaders with slower competitors, and the report does not give the method or period. A retailer starting from a controlled process will see less than one starting from guesswork. Plan your business case on your own pilot, with the cost of inaccurate forecasts in mind, which we cover in[the hidden cost of inaccurate sales forecasts](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/the-hidden-cost-of-inaccurate-sales-forecasts) .


## How to pilot inventory planning software before you commit


A pilot compares what the software recommends with real decisions on a narrow slice of your assortment. Six to eight weeks is usually enough to see a pattern.


1. **Pick one category with enough sales history.** A category with 100 to 300 products and a stable supplier base is a good test. Avoid one dominated by new launches.
2. **Freeze the baseline.** Record the orders your buyers actually place, and the stockouts and overstock they produce, so you have a comparison.
3. **Run the tool in shadow mode first.** Let it generate recommendations without placing them, and compare them with buyer decisions each week.
4. **Review the disagreements.** For every large gap, decide who was right and why. This teaches you more about the tool than the average result does.
5. **Measure service level and stock together.** A tool that cuts stock by pushing stockouts up has not improved anything. Track availability, days inventory outstanding (DIO), and forecast error such as weighted mean absolute percentage error (WMAPE) side by side. The wider set of network metrics is covered in our piece on[which KPIs to track for networked inventory](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/managing-networked-inventory-which-kpis-to-track-for-effective-control) .
6. **Decide on the actions in advance.** Agree who can accept, change, or reject a recommendation, and by when, before the pilot begins.


Rosa leads supply planning for a pharmacy network and ran a shadow pilot on 150 fast-moving products for eight weeks. Her buyers had placed their usual orders. Comparing afterwards, she found that the recommended orders would have avoided 11 of the 19 stockouts recorded, and that most of the differences sat in six products with erratic supplier lead times. (Rosa is an illustrative example.) That told her where to start and where to fix supplier data first.


## FAQ


### What is inventory planning software?


It is software that sets stock targets and recommends orders and transfers for each product and location, using a demand forecast, lead times, and service level goals. Planners review the recommendations and approve them rather than building each plan by hand.


### What is the difference between inventory planning and inventory management?


Inventory management is the record of what you hold and what moved. Planning adds a forecast-driven decision layer on top of it, and it reads its data from the management system, so most retailers run both.


### Can I plan inventory in Excel?


For a small assortment, yes. The formulas are the same. Spreadsheets get hard to maintain when you plan thousands of product and variant combinations across many locations and need to refresh targets as demand and lead times change.


### What features should inventory planning software have?


At minimum: forecasts by product and location, safety stock and reorder point calculation using lead time variability, replenishment and allocation recommendations, and an exception view that ranks the products needing attention. Integration with your ERP and sales data matters as much as any feature.


### How long does it take to implement inventory planning software?


It depends mostly on data readiness. Clean product, lead time, and stock data shortens it considerably. Ask each vendor how long it takes to produce a first plan on your own data, and use a shadow pilot to confirm the answer.


## Conclusion


Inventory planning software is worth evaluating when your reorder rules no longer reflect how products and locations actually behave. Test it on your own data, judge it by the decisions it changes, and treat published benefit figures as upper limits.
